source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Extraneous factors in judicial decisions
finding: Israeli parole judges ruled favorably about 65% of the time at the start of each of three daily sessions. The rate fell toward zero by the end and jumped back after food breaks. Authors suggest mental depletion.
numbers: 1,112 rulings (count taken from Glockner 2016); abstract: about 65% falls to nearly zero within a session, returns to about 65% after a break. Only the abstract was read this session; the full text is not open access.
quote: The percentage of favorable rulings drops gradually from ≈65% to nearly zero within each decision session
limits: Case order was not randomised by the researchers. Abstract only. Later critiques (b02 to b06) explain most of the pattern without fatigue.
agent_relevance: The founding result is a weak basis for a fatigue guardrail. Treat order drift as a hypothesis to test in the agent itself.

source: Glockner (2016) The irrational hungry judge effect revisited: simulations reveal that the magnitude of the effect is overestimated
finding: A simulation shows a fully rational judge would produce a similar drop. Favorable rulings take longer than unfavorable ones. A judge who avoids starting long cases just before a break, or who runs out of time, leaves mostly short (unfavorable) cases at the end of a session.
numbers: Favorable rulings took M=7.37 min (SD 5.11), unfavorable M=5.21 min (SD 4.97). Simulation: 10,000 randomly ordered cases, base rate 36% favorable and 64% unfavorable, 60-min session limit, favorable mean 8.2 vs unfavorable 5.8 min. With 5 minutes left only 12% of favorable cases still fit vs 46% of unfavorable. Result: strongly falling favorable rate by decision number, similar in size to the original.
quote: An effect of similar magnitude would be produced by a (hypothetical) rational judge who plans ahead minimally
limits: A simulation shows a possible artifact, not proof that it is the whole cause. Parameters come from the original paper's summary numbers, not raw data. Estimates get unstable for high decision numbers (few observations).
agent_relevance: Order drift can be a selection artifact when the amount of work per item depends on the outcome. The agent should check whether late-in-run items differ in kind before blaming fatigue.

source: Glockner (2016) effect size and mechanism plausibility check
finding: Glockner converts the headline drop into a standard effect size and compares it with the depletion literature. The drop is far larger than any depletion effect known.
numbers: Drop from 65% to 5% in the last trial = odds ratio 35 or d = 1.96. Meta-analytic depletion effect d = 0.10 to 0.25 (publication-bias corrected, Carter and McCullough 2013). Multi-lab ego-depletion replication (23 labs, N = 2,142) d = 0.04, not different from zero (Hagger and Chatzisarantis 2016).
limits: d = 1.96 is described as more than twice the conventional limit for large effects. Argument from plausibility, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Fatigue from repeated decisions has no solid human mechanism at this scale. For an LLM agent, any fatigue guardrail must be justified by its own measured drift.

source: Glockner (2016) non-random case order and rival explanations
finding: Rival accounts of the order pattern: (1) cases are not randomly ordered; unrepresented prisoners usually go last and are less likely to get parole; (2) the weakest cases drop out of late slots; (3) judges plan breaks to finish case sets. Weinshall-Margel and Shapard (2011) reached the first view from interviews with people in the parole process.
numbers: Sessions in the original show 10 to 13 cases in the plot; completed cases per session range from 2 to 283. Original authors' reply says the downward trend holds when controlling for attorney representation, but Glockner notes they did not report whether the size of the effect stays the same.
limits: Raw data were not public at the time; evidence is interview-based plus simulation. The original authors dispute the confounding explanation.
agent_relevance: Order effects need randomised order to test. In our agent loop, shuffle item order across runs before claiming an order effect.

source: Lakens (2017) Impossibly hungry judges
finding: Lakens argues the effect is too large to be a real psychological effect. A d near 2 matches the height gap between men and women, which would be obvious in everyday life. Comments raise the case-order confound.
numbers: d = 1.96, odds ratio 35 (from Glockner). Benchmarks: jury verdict effect d = 1.62; very large psychological effects are near d = 1.5 to 2.3 and mostly close to tautologies.
limits: A blog post, not peer-reviewed. Implausibility argument only; the confound discussion appears in comments.
agent_relevance: Use the implausibility test as a sanity check on any big effect in our own results: if the size is absurd, look for an artifact.

source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Reply to Weinshall-Margel and Shapard: extraneous factors in judicial decisions persist
finding: The original authors replied to a letter that challenged the study. Only the record was read (PNAS 108:E834). The challenge is described in b04 from Glockner.
numbers: No numbers read from the reply; Berthet (2021) cites Weinshall-Margel and Shapard (2011) as a 'but see' against the fatigue reading.
limits: Not opened beyond the record. The Weinshall-Margel and Shapard letter itself was not read.
agent_relevance: Same as b04: order effects need design control.

source: Berthet (2021) The impact of cognitive biases on professionals' decision-making: a review of four occupational areas
finding: Review of cognitive-bias studies in management, finance, medicine and law. For judges, anchoring is the best-supported bias. It notes the Danziger result is contested.
numbers: Enough and Mussweiler (2001) sentencing study: prosecutor demand of 34 months gave a mean of 24.41 months vs 17.64 months for a 12-month demand (review text says 8 months longer; the means differ by 6.77). Guthrie et al. (2001) damages: $1,249,000 without the motion vs $882,000 after ruling on the pre-trial jurisdiction motion. Effect independent of perceived relevance and judge experience.
limits: Narrative review. The 8 months vs 6.77 months mismatch is in the review text itself; check against the original.
agent_relevance: Numeric anchors shape expert output even when irrelevant. An agent doing numeric estimates should make an anchor-blind first pass.

source: Bystranowski et al. (2021) Anchoring effect in legal decision-making: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of numeric anchoring in legal decisions confirms a robust anchoring effect, with some evidence of publication bias and some moderation by legal expertise and anchor relevance.
numbers: 29 studies, 93 effect sizes, N = 8,549. With control group: d = 0.58 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.73). Without control group: d = 0.91 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.12).
limits: Abstract only. Moderator results described as preliminary; publication bias possible.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is the one judicial bias with strong meta-analytic support. Prioritise an anchoring guardrail over a fatigue guardrail.

source: Englich, Mussweiler, Strack (2006) Playing dice with criminal sentences (as cited by Berthet 2021)
finding: Anchoring on sentencing demand persisted even when the demand was set by a dice throw, so experts were anchored by information they knew was random.
numbers: No numbers read directly; Berthet (2021) states the dice-throw anchor still moved expert sentences. Englich et al. (2005) found the defense counter-demand is itself anchored on the prosecutor's.
limits: Cited through a review, not opened. Exact means, N and experience effects not checked.
agent_relevance: Even transparently arbitrary anchors move expert output. Telling an agent to ignore an anchor is not enough (see b23, b24).

source: Chen, Moskowitz, Shue (2016) Decision making under the gambler's fallacy: evidence from asylum judges, loan officers and baseball umpires
finding: A different order effect is better supported than the fatigue story. Decisions are negatively autocorrelated: after a grant, a judge is less likely to grant the next case, with no link to case merit. The effect is larger for moderate and less experienced judges.
numbers: US asylum judges: 0.5 percentage points less likely to grant after a previous grant (unconditional); 1.1 pp for non-extreme judges; up to 3.3 pp for moderate judges on same-day cases of the same type. After a streak of two grants, 5.5 pp less likely. Loan officers: up to 9% of decisions reversed due to negative autocorrelation. Umpires: 1.5 pp less likely to call a strike after the previous one.
limits: Asylum case order is not fully random; authors argue most non-random ordering would bias toward positive correlation. Loan officer field experiment had random order and accuracy pay; effect weakens with stronger incentives and slower review.
agent_relevance: Sequential contrast effects are real in repeated judgment. An agent grading a list of items one after another could show this. Test: shuffle and rerun.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig, Mullainathan (2018) Human decisions and machine predictions
finding: Bail judges differ widely in leniency and a model that predicts the judge's own decisions does better than the judge. The authors read the gap as noise, not hidden skill.
numbers: Most lenient quintile of judges released 82.9% of defendants; less lenient quintiles released 6.6, 9.6, 13.5 and 22.3 percentage points fewer. Algorithm at the same jailing rate could cut crime by 14.4% to 24.7%, or cut jail rates by 18.5% to 41.9% at no more crime. Cases were quasi-randomly assigned to judges.
quote: the net result is to create noise, not signal
limits: Bounds depend on assumptions about what unseen defendants would do. Unobserved case features could carry real signal.
agent_relevance: A simple consistent rule beat the average expert's inconsistent judgment. Supports a scaffold that forces a stable rubric.

source: Clancy et al. (1981) sentencing study as summarised on the Wikipedia page for Noise (Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein 2021)
finding: Between-judge noise in sentencing is large. Independent judges given the same fictive cases disagreed widely. The book separates level noise, stable pattern noise and occasion noise and says noise usually exceeds bias.
numbers: 208 criminal judges, 16 fictive cases: unanimous on imprisonment in only 3 of 16; one case averaged 1.1 prison years but one recommendation was 15 years. Insurance underwriters, 5 fictive customers: median premiums varied by 55%. Psychiatrists agreed on diagnosis in about half of 426 patients. Interviewers disagreed on the best candidate about 25% of the time.
limits: Secondary source (encyclopedia page), not the book. Proportions of noise types are tentative per the page.
agent_relevance: A noise audit is the right test for our agent: run the same item many times and measure spread. Spread is a cost even when the mean is right.

source: Chen and Philippe (2020) birthdays and judges; Simonsohn (2007) clouds and admissions (as cited on the Noise page)
finding: Occasion-noise examples listed without figures: French judges are more lenient on defendants' birthdays; admissions decisions shift with cloudy vs sunny days.
numbers: Only n = 682 for the weather study was given on the page; no effect sizes read.
limits: Cited secondhand with no numbers. Small irrelevant-cue effects have a poor replication record in other fields.
agent_relevance: Treat these as hypotheses for occasion noise, not firm facts.

source: Hagger et al. (2016) A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect
finding: A 23-lab preregistered replication found the ego-depletion effect small, with a confidence interval including zero. This is the mechanism the hungry-judge paper proposed.
numbers: k = 23 laboratories, total N = 2,141 (abstract). Glockner quotes d = 0.04, not different from zero.
limits: Abstract read only. One protocol (Sripada et al.) was used; other depletion tasks were not tested.
agent_relevance: Removes the mechanism that would make fatigue a natural property of repeated decisions.

source: Vohs et al. (2021) A multisite preregistered paradigmatic test of the ego-depletion effect
finding: A larger second replication again found no depletion effect. Depletion may be larger only for people who report more fatigue.
numbers: k = 36 labs, N = 3,531. Confirmatory d = 0.06 (nonsignificant). Bayes factor: data 4 times more likely under the null than under the informed-prior alternative. Exploratory full sample d = 0.08; larger for participants who reported more fatigue.
limits: Abstract only. Not a test in judges or in real decision work.
agent_relevance: Self-reported fatigue is the one open lead for any fatigue rule.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large language models are not fair evaluators
finding: Merely swapping the order of two answers flips the verdict of an LLM judge. Telling the judge not to let order matter did not stop it. Simple calibration steps help.
numbers: Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries with ChatGPT as judge, depending on order. GPT-4 judge conflict rate (verdict flips on swap) 37/80 = 46.3% for Vicuna vs ChatGPT. Accuracy vs human labels for a ChatGPT judge: vanilla 44.4%; multiple evidence plus balanced position 58.7%; with 20% human review 71.3% (human average 71.7%).
quote: even though the template emphasizes not letting the order affect the results
limits: 80 Vicuna-benchmark questions; two judge models; early-2023 model versions.
agent_relevance: A direct LLM analogue of a judicial order effect. Always evaluate both orders and average; a do-not-let-order-matter instruction is not a fix.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: LLM judges show position bias, verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias, yet strong judges agree with humans about as much as humans agree with each other.
numbers: Position consistency when order is swapped: GPT-4 65.0% (30.0% prefer first, 5.0% second); GPT-3.5 46.2% (50.0% prefer first); Claude-v1 23.8% (75.0% prefer first). Few-shot examples raised GPT-4 consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%. GPT-4 agreement with humans over 80%, same as human-human.
limits: High consistency does not imply high accuracy. Few-shot may add new biases and makes calls about 4 times costlier.
agent_relevance: Order bias is model-dependent and large for weaker models. Swap-and-agree is the cheap debias.

source: Lu, Bartolo, Moore, Riedel, Stenetorp (2022) Fantastically ordered prompts and where to find them
finding: The order of few-shot examples alone can move GPT-style models from near state-of-the-art to random guessing. The effect holds across model sizes and a good order for one model does not transfer to another.
numbers: All 24 permutations of 4 training samples tested on SST-2 across model sizes 0.1B to 175B; an entropy-based selection gives about 13% relative improvement over a wide range of tasks.
limits: Classification tasks with few-shot prompts, GPT-2 and GPT-3; instruction-tuned models not tested.
agent_relevance: Item order within the prompt is a pure noise source. Randomise or average over orders when measuring the agent.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs
finding: A benchmark (BiasBuster) of 13,465 prompts tests prompt-induced, sequential and inherent biases in four LLMs in a college admissions setting. Models show framing, group-attribution and primacy-like patterns. A self-debiasing rewrite of the prompt beat other fixes.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under reject framing than admit framing. Llama-2 7B classed 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Models chose early options (A, B) more than C plus D. When allowed to revise anchored decisions, Llama models changed 40% to 52% of decisions (GPT-3.5 5.2%, GPT-4 17.5%).
limits: Admissions vignettes, not court cases; four 2023 models. Few-shot debiasing often caused failure (admit/reject rate driven to 0 or 1). Awareness prompts only partly helped.
agent_relevance: Self-help (the model rewrites its own biased prompt) was the best debias tested, but only for high-capacity models. Avoid few-shot bias examples in the schema.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study
finding: LLMs are strongly anchored by hints in numeric estimates. Stronger models were more consistently anchored. Chain-of-thought, thoughts of principles, ignoring anchor hints and reflection did not fix it. Gathering hints from several angles did.
numbers: 62 questions; 162 answer-difference values across GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5; only 11 had the wrong sign relative to the hint direction. Average anchoring index for GPT-4 about 0.45 vs 0.61 in the human study the dataset came from.
limits: Preprint from authors at a Beijing school; dataset from a prior human forecasting study; time-period questions were less anchored. Mitigation results are mostly qualitative.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that ignore-the-anchor and CoT are insufficient. The schema should require independent estimates from different angles before any prior number is shown.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans?
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) shows the anchoring heuristic with random anchors, about as strongly as human participants.
numbers: Low-anchor mean estimate 20.83 (CI 13.92 to 27.74) for ChatGPT vs 22.5 for humans; high anchor 105.97 (CI 87.40 to 124.54) for ChatGPT vs 80.50 for humans. Low vs high: t(58) = 8.78 for ChatGPT, 5.55 for humans; ChatGPT vs humans in the high condition t(58) = 1.90, p = 0.06. A GPT-4 follow-up with 5 trials per condition gave means 22.0 vs 94.33.
limits: Single task (random number then estimate), GPT-3.5, small samples.
agent_relevance: Anchoring in the LLM is as large as in humans, so human debiasing research is a fair source of tests.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Justice or prejudice? Quantifying biases in LLM-as-a-judge
finding: CALM tests 12 biases in LLM judges. Position bias grows with the number of answer candidates, and most models score below 0.5 robustness on position. Strong models still show bias on some tasks.
numbers: 12 bias types; position robustness rate below 0.5 for most judge models with more candidates; self-enhancement bias found in most models.
limits: Metric is robustness under controlled edits to answers, not agreement with human judges.
agent_relevance: Randomise candidate order and use fewer candidates per comparison.

source: Large language models exhibit greater diagnostic anchoring than physicians in a forced-choice vignette study (2026)
finding: LLMs were more anchored than doctors by a misleading patient statement in clinical vignettes.
numbers: Anchor diagnosis ranked first: residents 17/80 (21.2%), attendings 2/20 (10.0%), LLMs 40/72 (55.6%). LLM odds vs residents OR 3.94 (95% CI 2.32 to 7.33). 9 vignette pairs; 8 LLMs; 20 residents and 5 attendings.
limits: Abstract only; forced-choice ranking, not open-ended; small human sample.
agent_relevance: In forced-choice tasks LLMs may be more anchored than experts. Do not assume the human literature overstates the risk for the agent.

source: The Hungry Judge effect on prostate MRI reporting (2024)
finding: A large retrospective radiology dataset finds a tiny association between hour of day and PI-RADS scores.
numbers: 35,004 prostate MRI interpretations by 26 radiologists over 8 years; hour-of-day coefficient beta2 = 0.005 on mean PI-RADS (p-value cut off in the abstract I read).
limits: Abstract only. Retrospective; case mix across hours not shown. Authors call the effect small.
agent_relevance: Time-of-day drift in experts is real but small in a clean large sample, nowhere near d = 2.

source: Time-of-day changes in physician clinical decision making: a retrospective study (2021, PLOS ONE)
finding: Doctors ordered more tests in the first hour of the day than the last hour. Effects vary a lot between doctors and clinics.
numbers: 3,342 appointments, 20 attending physicians, five clinics; 16 of 20 physicians ordered more tests in the first vs last hour (sign test p = 0.012); 4 and 6 physicians individually significant for tests and diagnoses.
limits: Retrospective chart review, abstract only; case mix may differ between hours.
agent_relevance: Time-of-day patterns are small and person-specific. A noise audit is more informative than a fatigue rule.

source: Chatziathanasiou (2022) Beware the lure of narratives: hungry judges should not motivate the use of artificial intelligence in law
finding: Argues the hungry-judge story is a poor reason for using AI in courts because the evidence is weak. Cited 26 times per Crossref.
numbers: No numbers read; the page could not be fetched this session.
limits: Not opened. Content stated only from its title and the Crossref record.
agent_relevance: Verify the paper text before use.

source: Berthet (2021) judges' numeric translation step (Wissler et al. 1999; Hart et al. 1997)
finding: Noise is concentrated where qualitative judgments become numbers. Severity ratings are consistent; the amount or sentence varies widely.
numbers: Review text: qualitative judgments show a high degree of consistency (Wissler et al. 1999) but variability is large for non-economic and punitive damages and sentences.
limits: Review statement. Original numbers not reported in the review.
agent_relevance: Ask the agent to rank or bin first and convert to a number with a fixed table.

source: Assessing judges' use and awareness of cognitive heuristic decision-making (2025, Frontiers in Cognition)
finding: A questionnaire of 52 Greek judges found four heuristic factors (availability, confirmation, representativeness, anchoring). Judges who scored higher on the cognitive reflection test reported using anchoring more.
numbers: N = 52 judges (20 men, mean age 45.5). Spearman rho = 0.29, p = 0.04 between CRT score and reported anchoring use.
limits: Small sample; self-report, not behaviour; one country.
agent_relevance: Awareness and reflection do not remove the bias; reflective people may even report more anchoring use.
